## The segment store

The coordinate space maps onto physical memory as a flat array: 11,172 slots of 16 bits each, addressed by the 14-bit offset from the decoder. The single-port SRAM macro is configured for SkyWater 130nm, and the macro generation is pending an OpenRAM PDK install. What is verified today is a behavioral model of the same address map and read/write behavior, checked exhaustively over all 11,172 slots with the 5,212 reserved addresses reading zero. The OpenRAM configuration is:

```python
#| eval: false
word_size = 16          # one Hangul code point per word
num_words = 11172       # full Tagma space: U+AC00..U+D7A3, 19 x 21 x 28
num_rw_ports = 1        # single read-write port
tech_name = "sky130"
```

The full space is about 22 KB of raw storage, or 44 to 89 KB with values, depending on the value width. 11,172 is not a power of two; if the PDK flow requires one, the fallback is 16,384 words (2^14) with 5,212 reserved entries, since the 14-bit address space covers the valid range either way.

## Latency: the honest comparison

Three measured paths are compared below. The software numbers come from the benchmark center `sw/rust/benches/bench_hw.rs`; the hardware number is the post place-and-route critical path on the UP5K. The comparison is shown in Figure @fig-hw-decode.

:::{ layout-ncol=1 }

{{< include ../_include/bench/fig-hw-decode.qmd >}}

:::

The per-operation latency comparison is the central finding of this document:

| Path | Latency | Note |
|------|---------|------|
| `CoordSpace.get` (software) | 0.38 ns | whole space in L1 cache |
| `Coord::to_axes` (software) | 1.44 ns | reference decode |
| HW decoder (UP5K PnR) | 59.55 ns | worst-case critical path at 16.79 MHz |

For the N=1 dense case, hardware is not a speedup. The entire working set fits in L1 cache, and the software already runs at memory speed. A hardware SRAM at FPGA clock rates cannot beat that, and GHz-class SRAM would require a leading-edge ASIC whose mask cost starts in the millions of dollars. Chasing L1 speed in hardware is solving a problem the software already solved.

## Where hardware wins

The value of the hardware realization is on other axes:

| Axis | Software | Hardware |
|------|----------|----------|
| Range query over an axis | iterative descent over a tree or a scan | the bounds are computed from the code, so the iteration is an increment |
| Index storage | a separate structure beside the records | none, because the key is the order and the range address |
| Energy per access | host CPU pipeline and cache hierarchy | about 3.0 pJ per decode at 12 MHz, from the Sky130 flow at the workload's measured activity |
| Latency determinism | cache-dependent, variable | fixed, independent of the input: one cycle combinational, four pipelined |
| Physical embedding | impossible | the primitive becomes a device, the chton signal-layer vision |
| Streaming throughput | per-op overhead in software | one code point per clock; 148.77 MHz register to register on the ECP5, 140 MHz verified against the `tagma_core` checksum on the board |

The structural case is the first two rows and it is derived rather than measured: with records keyed by code, the key is the sort order and the range address, so a range walk is an increment and no index exists to store or to search. That is what the segment store would exercise, and it is the part not yet on a device.

The throughput case is narrower and is measured. It appears at N greater than 1, where software falls back to sparse trees (0.87 to 53 ns per operation), and in embedded or IO paths where energy and determinism dominate over raw speed. The streaming realization is measured rather than projected: a four-stage pipeline emits one code point per clock, closes at 148.77 MHz on the ECP5, and reproduces the `tagma_core` checksum on the device at every rate up to 140 MHz. At that rate it still sits below the L1 path, 140 million code points per second against 2.6 billion accesses per second, so the case it serves is a continuous stream with a fixed cost per code point rather than a faster dense lookup.

## Open questions

The Sky130 standard cell flow is set up and runs in CI (`hw` job in the syntagma repository): ORFS on the x86 runner produces the area, timing, and power report for the registered demo top, plus the pure decoder gate count via `yosys stat -liberty`. The flow runs on x86 and on Apple Silicon under Rosetta; the default-on kepler-formal LEC step crashes on both and is disabled in the design config (see the syntagma devlog entry). The VCD activity trace from simulation (`make sim-trace-demo`) is the input for the power estimation, and the figure it produces is provisional: see the synthesis document for the run-to-run difference that is not yet explained. The OpenRAM SRAM macro generation remains pending a PDK install.
